title: Sensor coverage and winter chlorophyll changes cause most of the 1998-2025 bloom-start advance in merged ocean-colour data for the North Atlantic and North Pacific; bloom peaks follow spring SST
abstract: Question: how much of the bloom-timing trend in the merged ESA OC-CCI v6.0 ocean-colour record comes from the change in sensor coverage, and how much follows sea surface temperature? Approach: 8-day chlorophyll (4 km, every 6th pixel) in 1-degree boxes in the North Atlantic (40-70N, 60W-0) and North Pacific (38-62N, 145E-125W), 1998-2025; threshold phenology (median x 1.05); a fixed SeaWiFS-era observation window (composites seen in at least 2 of 1998-2001) to remove the coverage gain; a synthetic test with each year's real mask on one fixed seasonal cycle; NOAA OISST v2.1 monthly SST. Results: January coverage increased from 0.20 to about 0.33 (Atlantic) and 0.21 to 0.55 (Pacific), mostly at sensor additions in 2003 and 2016. Bloom initiation advanced -5.2 [-7.6, -2.9] and -15.4 [-19.3, -11.4] days per decade in all merged data, and -3.7 and -10.1 in the fixed window (coverage part 29% and 34%). Inside the window, January chlorophyll rose in steps (+0.1 log10 Atlantic, +0.07 Pacific), so more starts fell in January. With censored box-years removed, or a year-specific threshold in strong-bloom boxes, the initiation trend was not different from zero in either basin. Peak dates had a small coverage effect. Warm springs came with earlier peaks in both basins (-3.5 [-5.5, -1.7] and -4.6 [-7.5, -1.5] days per 1 C, detrended). The Pacific peak advanced -4.1 [-7.0, -1.3] days per decade, about 43% of which the SST relation predicts; the Atlantic peak did not change clearly, and its spring SST did not change. Limitations: merged retrievals, so the winter step can be a sensor artefact or real; censoring removal and threshold changes are exploratory; SST is a proxy for stratification.
